50	Training alters joint power distributions during running in
51	National Football League Draft Preparation Players
52	G. Monique Mokha, Marissa Bonsangue, ToniAnn Brezina and Jacob Haberer
53	Exercise and Sport Science, Nova Southeastern University, Fort Lauderdale, FL, USA
54	
55	
56	    ABSTRACT                                                                   ARTICLE HISTORY
57	    The aim of this study was to compare joint-specific contributions to       Received 4 October 2024
58	    total lower limb joint power during a speed run in American style          Accepted 23 April 2025
59	    football players before and after a 6-week National Football League        KEYWORDS
60	    (NFL) draft preparation camp. Fifty-two players performed one 5-           American style football; team
61	    second treadmill run at 5.5–6.5 m/s before and after camp. Speed           sport running; kinetics;
62	    was consistent between tests. Bilateral hip, knee, and ankle power         performance; joint power
63	    generation (positive) and absorption (negative) were calculated
64	    from kinematics and kinetics using inverse dynamics. Negative
65	    total limb power decreased for both limbs, significantly for the
66	    left (Z = −2.113, p = .035, r = .30) due to significant decreases in
67	    negative ankle power bilaterally (left, Z = −1.967, p = .049, r = .27;
68	    right, Z = −2.623, p = .009, r = .36). The contribution of negative left
69	    hip power significantly increased (Z = −2.398, p = .016, r = .31).
70	    While no other significant changes in positive or negative joint-
71	    specific magnitudes or contributions occurred, there were general
72	    distal-to-proximal shifts in joint power contributions. Players appear
73	    to have adopted more energy efficient running through moderate
74	    joint-specific mechanistic training adaptations such as a reduction
75	    in ankle power absorption.
76	
77	
78	
79	Introduction
80	Sprint speed is a key skill for American style football players. Players seeking to be drafted
81	by the National Football League (NFL) showcase their linear speed running abilities in
82	the 36.6 m (40 yard) dash at an annual combine. The combine is a weeklong invitation-
83	only event where top university prospects (approximately 300) perform physical and
84	mental assessments for personnel of the league’s 32 teams. Research shows drafted
85	players perform better in the 36.6 m sprint than non-drafted players (Sierer et al.,
86	2008) and superior performance is associated with higher draft position (Tucker &
87	Black, 2023). Combine invitees and other eligible players attend specialised training
88	camps leading up to the NFL draft to prepare. Linear speed mechanics is one focus of
89	these camps since players must transition from game play running to test performance
90	running. Mokha et al. (2021) showed that 36.6 m time significantly improved in a group
91	of American style football players participating in a six-week NFL draft preparation
92	camp. Players appeared to accomplish this through decreasing ground contact time (pre,
93	177 ± 3.2 vs. post, 168 ± 2.2 ms) and increasing average vertical ground reaction force
94	
95	CONTACT G. Monique Mokha                gm588@nova.edu
96	© 2025 International Society of Biomechanics in Sports
97	 2      G. M. MOKHA ET AL.
98	
99	
100	(vGRF) (pre, 1.5 ± 0.3 vs. post, 1.6 ± 0.1 BW). These changes represent hallmarks of
101	higher velocity runs (Colyer et al., 2018; Morin et al., 2011; Weyand, 2017; Weyand et al.,
102	2010). While these changes alone would not be enough to improve the participants’
103	linear speed in the 36.6 m dash, they shed light on how foot-ground kinetics are modifi­
104	able in elite American style football players and provide foundation for further kinetic
105	analysis.
106	    During running, mechanical work must be done to rotate limb segments, restore
107	energy lost during early ground contact, and propel the body forward. Given that ground
108	contact times for sprinting range from 85 to 190 ms (Mattes et al., 2021; Numella et al.,
109	2007; Weyand et al., 2010), the ability to perform work in a short time is vital and gives
110	rise to examining joint power. Decrements in the capacity of the muscles to produce
111	adequate power during running have been shown to negatively impact sprint speed
112	(Sánchez-Sánchez et al., 2018; Small et al., 2009). Joint power is distinguished from
113	system power where system power represents the rate at which the mechanical work is
114	done on an external load and may veil the power contributions from the individual joints
115	(Moir et al., 2012). Joint powers represent the rate at which mechanical work is accom­
116	plished at the joints providing estimates of muscle activity (Pires et al., 2014; Riddick &
117	Kuo, 2022). Joint power magnitudes have been shown to increase as running speeds
118	increase (Belli et al., 2002; Khassetarash et al., 2020). While improvements in speed and
119	system power performance have been documented in American style football players
120	undergoing training (Crawley et al., 2024; Gillen et al., 2024; Hoffman et al., 2004, 2009;
121	Moore & Fry, 2007), the joint level mechanisms underlying adaptation have not been
122	explored.
123	    Positive joint power is primarily generated by concentric muscle contractions and
124	potential strain energy is released. Most of the positive power (>60%) is generated at the
125	ankle joint during ground contact when the plantar flexors (gastrocnemius and soleus
126	muscles) contract to propel the body forward (Swinnen et al., 2021). Sanno et al. (2018)
127	reported that prolonged running at near maximal effort shifted the distribution of
128	positive joint work proximally in recreational but not competitive distance runners
129	suggesting that shifting positive joint work from the ankle plantar flexors towards hip
130	extensors could be detrimental to running economy. This shift has also been reported to
131	occur in middle-distance runners completing an exhaustive run (181 ± 42 s to exhaus­
132	tion) and in older runners as a sign of performance decline (Kim & Park, 2022).
133	Furthermore, hip muscle activation during the swing phase consumes energy, leading
134	to the estimated relative contribution of leg swing to the energetic cost of 7–11%
135	(Swinnen et al., 2021). While these findings appear to indicate that a distal-to-proximal
136	shift may be deleterious, it may be a necessary adaptation to faster running speeds. For
137	example, the hip’s contribution to average positive power in both stance and swing
138	phases has been shown to significantly increase with faster running speeds (i.e.,
139	6.0–9.0 m/s) (Schache et al., 2011, 2015). AminiAghdam et al. (2021) found that anterior
140	trunk lean shifted power from the knee to the hip during level and uneven running at
141	speeds of 3.5 m/s.
142	    Negative joint work and power are primarily generated by eccentric muscle contrac­
143	tions where potential strain energy is stored and mechanical energy is reduced (DeVita et
144	al., 2007). Since eccentric muscle contractions are associated with greater muscle damage
145	(Hashizume et al., 2017), negative joint power is of particular interest. Negative power is
146	                                                                  SPORTS BIOMECHANICS       3
147	
148	
149	produced during the braking phase of running and is controlled reflexively by the leg
150	extensors (Belli et al., 2002). The knee and ankle joints contribute greatly to limb power
151	absorption compared to the hip joint (Hashizume et al., 2018). Belli et al. (2002) found
152	the overall negative work absorbed at initial contact was lower than the positive power
153	produced at end contact point, especially at the knee joint. The elongation time of the
154	ankle and knee muscles is short and has been attributed to high ankle joint stiffness
155	preventing yielding of the centre of mass at initial contact (Belli et al., 2002). It is not
156	known how participating in a performance preparation program affects this mechanism.
157	   Magnitudes and percentage contributions of joint power to total limb power may be
158	sensitive to training aimed at improving linear speed mechanics even in highly trained
159	athletes. Exploring joint level mechanics in American style football players may provide
160	insight into the mechanistic adaptations of running performance that may carry over to
161	other team sports where running is integral such as rugby, football (soccer), or Australian
162	rules football. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to assess the changes in joint
163	power magnitude and distribution during a high-speed run before and after a six-week
164	training camp in American style football players. We hypothesised that speed focused
165	exercises presented in training camp would redistribute the power contributions from
166	the lower limb joints, characterised by a reduction of power from the ankle even if
167	treadmill speed were kept uniform. To test the hypothesis, we used an inverse dynamic
168	approach to calculate individual joint and total limb powers during a high-speed run
169	before and after participation in training camp.

172	Materials and methods
173	Experimental approach
174	This study was part of a larger study monitoring pre-post changes in body composition,
175	and vertical jump and speed running mechanics over the duration of a six-week training
176	camp designed to prepare eligible American style football players for the NFL draft.
177	Camp was divided into three microcycles that included drill specificity training, player
178	position specificity training, resistance training and recovery-based movement (e.g.,
179	pool, soft tissue massage). The study procedures were conducted at the start of training
180	camp and six weeks later at the end of training camp. We obtained written informed
181	consent that was approved by the university’s Institutional Review Board (#2018-684)
182	and the study complied with the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association,
183	2013).

190	receivers, tight ends, defensive linemen) and had competed for different university
191	teams in the United States. All participants had just completed their collegiate football
192	season, were active players training 5-6× per week, and were cleared by licenced medical
193	staff to participate in the study. All 75 completed the testing, but 23 were excluded due to

Introduction
Sprint speed is a key skill for American style football players. Players seeking to be drafted
by the National Football League (NFL) showcase their linear speed running abilities in
the 36.6 m (40 yard) dash at an annual combine. The combine is a weeklong invitation-
only event where top university prospects (approximately 300) perform physical and
mental assessments for personnel of the league’s 32 teams. Research shows drafted
players perform better in the 36.6 m sprint than non-drafted players (Sierer et al.,
2008) and superior performance is associated with higher draft position (Tucker &
Black, 2023). Combine invitees and other eligible players attend specialised training
camps leading up to the NFL draft to prepare. Linear speed mechanics is one focus of
these camps since players must transition from game play running to test performance
running. Mokha et al. (2021) showed that 36.6 m time significantly improved in a group
of American style football players participating in a six-week NFL draft preparation
camp. Players appeared to accomplish this through decreasing ground contact time (pre,
177 ± 3.2 vs. post, 168 ± 2.2 ms) and increasing average vertical ground reaction force

CONTACT G. Monique Mokha                gm588@nova.edu
© 2025 International Society of Biomechanics in Sports
 2      G. M. MOKHA ET AL.


(vGRF) (pre, 1.5 ± 0.3 vs. post, 1.6 ± 0.1 BW). These changes represent hallmarks of
higher velocity runs (Colyer et al., 2018; Morin et al., 2011; Weyand, 2017; Weyand et al.,
2010). While these changes alone would not be enough to improve the participants’
linear speed in the 36.6 m dash, they shed light on how foot-ground kinetics are modifi­
able in elite American style football players and provide foundation for further kinetic
analysis.
    During running, mechanical work must be done to rotate limb segments, restore
energy lost during early ground contact, and propel the body forward. Given that ground
contact times for sprinting range from 85 to 190 ms (Mattes et al., 2021; Numella et al.,
2007; Weyand et al., 2010), the ability to perform work in a short time is vital and gives
rise to examining joint power. Decrements in the capacity of the muscles to produce
adequate power during running have been shown to negatively impact sprint speed
(Sánchez-Sánchez et al., 2018; Small et al., 2009). Joint power is distinguished from
system power where system power represents the rate at which the mechanical work is
done on an external load and may veil the power contributions from the individual joints
(Moir et al., 2012). Joint powers represent the rate at which mechanical work is accom­
plished at the joints providing estimates of muscle activity (Pires et al., 2014; Riddick &
Kuo, 2022). Joint power magnitudes have been shown to increase as running speeds
increase (Belli et al., 2002; Khassetarash et al., 2020). While improvements in speed and
system power performance have been documented in American style football players
undergoing training (Crawley et al., 2024; Gillen et al., 2024; Hoffman et al., 2004, 2009;
Moore & Fry, 2007), the joint level mechanisms underlying adaptation have not been
explored.
    Positive joint power is primarily generated by concentric muscle contractions and
potential strain energy is released. Most of the positive power (>60%) is generated at the
ankle joint during ground contact when the plantar flexors (gastrocnemius and soleus
muscles) contract to propel the body forward (Swinnen et al., 2021). Sanno et al. (2018)
reported that prolonged running at near maximal effort shifted the distribution of
positive joint work proximally in recreational but not competitive distance runners
suggesting that shifting positive joint work from the ankle plantar flexors towards hip
extensors could be detrimental to running economy. This shift has also been reported to
occur in middle-distance runners completing an exhaustive run (181 ± 42 s to exhaus­
tion) and in older runners as a sign of performance decline (Kim & Park, 2022).
Furthermore, hip muscle activation during the swing phase consumes energy, leading
to the estimated relative contribution of leg swing to the energetic cost of 7–11%
(Swinnen et al., 2021). While these findings appear to indicate that a distal-to-proximal
shift may be deleterious, it may be a necessary adaptation to faster running speeds. For
example, the hip’s contribution to average positive power in both stance and swing
phases has been shown to significantly increase with faster running speeds (i.e.,
6.0–9.0 m/s) (Schache et al., 2011, 2015). AminiAghdam et al. (2021) found that anterior
trunk lean shifted power from the knee to the hip during level and uneven running at
speeds of 3.5 m/s.
    Negative joint work and power are primarily generated by eccentric muscle contrac­
tions where potential strain energy is stored and mechanical energy is reduced (DeVita et
al., 2007). Since eccentric muscle contractions are associated with greater muscle damage
(Hashizume et al., 2017), negative joint power is of particular interest. Negative power is
                                                                  SPORTS BIOMECHANICS       3


produced during the braking phase of running and is controlled reflexively by the leg
extensors (Belli et al., 2002). The knee and ankle joints contribute greatly to limb power
absorption compared to the hip joint (Hashizume et al., 2018). Belli et al. (2002) found
the overall negative work absorbed at initial contact was lower than the positive power
produced at end contact point, especially at the knee joint. The elongation time of the
ankle and knee muscles is short and has been attributed to high ankle joint stiffness
preventing yielding of the centre of mass at initial contact (Belli et al., 2002). It is not
known how participating in a performance preparation program affects this mechanism.
   Magnitudes and percentage contributions of joint power to total limb power may be
sensitive to training aimed at improving linear speed mechanics even in highly trained
athletes. Exploring joint level mechanics in American style football players may provide
insight into the mechanistic adaptations of running performance that may carry over to
other team sports where running is integral such as rugby, football (soccer), or Australian
rules football. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to assess the changes in joint
power magnitude and distribution during a high-speed run before and after a six-week
training camp in American style football players. We hypothesised that speed focused
exercises presented in training camp would redistribute the power contributions from
the lower limb joints, characterised by a reduction of power from the ankle even if
treadmill speed were kept uniform. To test the hypothesis, we used an inverse dynamic
approach to calculate individual joint and total limb powers during a high-speed run
before and after participation in training camp.


Materials and methods
Experimental approach
This study was part of a larger study monitoring pre-post changes in body composition,
and vertical jump and speed running mechanics over the duration of a six-week training
camp designed to prepare eligible American style football players for the NFL draft.
Camp was divided into three microcycles that included drill specificity training, player
position specificity training, resistance training and recovery-based movement (e.g.,
pool, soft tissue massage). The study procedures were conducted at the start of training
camp and six weeks later at the end of training camp. We obtained written informed
consent that was approved by the university’s Institutional Review Board (#2018-684)
and the study complied with the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association,
2013).


Participants
A sample of convenience of 75 adult American style football players were recruited from
a group of players enrolled in a specialised training camp at a local performance centre
for the 2024 NFL draft. Players represented a variety of field positions (e.g., wide
receivers, tight ends, defensive linemen) and had competed for different university
teams in the United States. All participants had just completed their collegiate football
season, were active players training 5-6× per week, and were cleared by licenced medical
staff to participate in the study. All 75 completed the testing, but 23 were excluded due to
 4           G. M. MOKHA ET AL.


not achieving treadmill running speed of at least 5.5 m/s for trial duration (n = 11),
retroreflective markers falling off during either the pre- or post-test (n = 7), or trials
that qualitatively were deemed an unnatural running pattern by the investigators (n = 5).
Data for 52 participants (age, 23.0 ± 0.9 yrs.; height, 1.85 ± 0.06 m; mass, 100.1 ± 19.6 kg)
are presented in this study.


Protocol
Participants reported to the Sports Performance and Gait Laboratory in groups of three
at a designated time over 2 ½ days at both the start and end of the six-week training
camp. The training camp was divided into three microcycles that included drill specificity
training, player position specificity training, resistance training and recovery-based
movement (e.g., pool, soft tissue massage). Table 1 presents specific drills used by the
coaches to improve linear speed mechanics. They were performed four times per week.
The repetitions varied with relevance to other training demands of a session but were
typically 5–10.
   During data collection, participants wore compression shorts and their own running
shoes. After explaining the study and procuring written informed consent, anthropo­
metric measures were obtained according to the specifications of Vicon Nexus Plug-in
Gait lower body model (Vicon, Centennial, CO, USA). These were used to estimate
segment masses and moments of inertia necessary for inverse dynamics. To increase
accuracy, the researchers used a felt tip marker to identify the anterior superior iliac
spines since these landmarks are used for pelvis width, leg length, and marker placement.
Following anthropometrics, participants completed a standardised 25-minute warm-up
led by a single coach consisting of dynamic stretching, muscle readiness and reactivity
exercises. Then, sixteen 14 mm retroreflective markers were placed bilaterally on the
participant’s pelvis and lower limbs according to the specifications of Vicon’s Plug-in
Gait lower body model and a local calibration was performed with the participant
standing in anatomical position. The running trial took place on an instrumented split
belt treadmill (Bertec Corporation, Columbus, OH, USA) with participants running on
one side with zero incline. Participants began by walking on the treadmill at 1.0 m/s for

2–3 minutes. Speed was increased 1 m/s in one second increments where 3-second pauses
occurred at jogging (~3.5 m/s) and fast jogging (~5.0 m/s) speeds to facilitate comfort.
When the participant reached preferred maximum speed (maximum speed allowed by
the treadmill was 6.5 m/s), they ran for 1- to 2-s before a 5-s recording was taken. This
capture time was selected to mimic most 36.6 m (40 yd) run durations at the NFL
combine. At the completion of the trial, participants transferred their weight to the
non-moving belt, and the running treadmill belt was decelerated to a stop. Mean running
speed was 6.4 m/s and the speed achieved at the pre-test was replicated at the post-test.
Only one running trial was collected at both testing sessions. Participants were instructed
to wear their same shoes to the post-test, but this was not assured by the researchers.


Instrumentation
Running kinematic and kinetic data were captured in a laboratory using a 10-camera 3D
motion analysis system (Vicon, Centennial, CO, USA) sampling at 120 hz and recorded
synchronously with an instrumented split belt treadmill (Bertec Corporation, Columbus,
OH, USA) collecting at 1000 hz. The motion analysis system was calibrated on the day of
each data collection session to an accuracy defined by a 3D residual below of .20 mm.
Lower limb length, pelvis and lower limb breadth, and total body mass were measured
using a common fibreglass tape measure, anthropometers (Lafayette Instruments,
Lafayette, IN, USA), and an InBody 270 multifrequency bioelectrical impedance device
(InBody USA, Cerritos, CA, USA), respectively. Height was self-reported.


Data processing
We compared the joint power absorbed (negative) and generated (positive) including the
percent distribution from the hip, knee, and ankle to total limb power between weeks one
and six of training camp. Power was derived from kinematic and kinetic data using
inverse dynamics with rigid body assumptions. Marker coordinates were labelled and gap
filled, and joint angles were calculated using Vicon Nexus software (ver. 2.15). Since
participants ran on one side of the split-belt treadmill, gait cycles were visually inspected
to identify left and right ground contact and foot-off events in the software based on
vertical ground reaction forces. This allowed for synchronisation of the GRF with the
motion capture data. Marker trajectories and ground reaction forces were filtered with a
low-pass third-order Butterworth filter with a cut-off frequency of 10 hz and 50 hz,
respectively.

computed in Vicon Nexus using the Newton-Euler approach of inverse dynamics. See
Equations 1 and 2 where Equation 2 is specific to the knee.

The timing of negative and positive power was defined by identifying the point of zero

Values were normalised to body mass (W/kg).


Statistical analysis
Means, standard deviations, and confidence intervals were calculated for peak positive
and negative ankle, knee, hip, and total power for both limbs normalised to the partici­
pant’s body mass. Then, to obtain the relative contribution of each joint’s positive power
to the total calculated, we divided the average power of each joint by the sum of the
average positive power of the hip, knee, and ankle. This was repeated for negative powers.
We screened the data for normality using a Shapiro-Wilk test. Results showed all knee
power values for both limbs departed significantly from normality, p ≤ .05. Therefore, the
non-parametric test, Wilcoxon Signed Rank was used to determine the mean differences
in the joint power variables between the pre- and post-test runs, p ≤ .05. These statistical
calculations were conducted using SPSS (ver. 29). Effect sizes (r) were also calculated for
the pairwise comparisons using the formula, r ¼ pjZffiNjffiffi (Pallant, 2020). An r effect size of 0.1
was considered small, 0.3 a medium effect, and 0.5 a large effect (Cohen, 2013).


Results
Figures 2 and 3 present mean and standard deviation values for pre- and post-test total limb
positive and negative power, respectively. There were no significant changes in total positive
power for left (Z = −0.073, p = .942, r = .01) or right (Z = −0.419, p = .675, r = .06) limbs.
Negative total power decreased for both limbs, and this was statistically significant for the
left (Z = −2.113, p = .035, r = .30) but not the right (Z = −1.776, p = .076, r = .25) limbs.




Figure 2. Pre- and post-test positive total joint power for left and right limbs.

Figure 3. Pre- and post-test negative total joint power for left and right limbs. *denotes significant
difference, p < .05.


   Table 2 presents the means, standard deviations, 95% confidence intervals (CI),
p levels, and effect sizes for positive and negative individual joint and power for left
and right limbs pre- and post-training camp. Negative ankle joint power significantly
decreased for the left (Z = −1.967) and right (Z = −2.623) limbs, p < .05. No other
significant changes occurred in positive or negative hip or knee joint powers (p > .05).
   Table 3 presents the means, standard deviations, 95% confidence intervals (CI),
p levels, and effect sizes of the relative contributions of positive and negative joint
power to total power for left and right limbs. Figures 3 and 4 depict the pre- and post-
test relative contribution of the ankle, knee, and hip to the total positive and negative
power for both limbs.
   While there was a general shift in positive joint power from distal-to-proximal for
both limbs (see Figures 3 and 4), these changes were not statistically significant. There
were no significant changes in the percent contribution for the hip (left, Z = −1.941; right,
Z = −1.640), knee (left, Z = −1.256; right, Z = −0.530), or ankle (left, Z = −0.914); right,
Z = −0.873) joints after six weeks of training, p > .05.
   For negative joint power contribution, there was also a shift from distal-to-proximal
(see Figures 4 and 5), and this was significant on the left limb. Specifically, the left hip
significantly changed (increased) (Z = −2.398,), p < .05. There were no significant
changes in the right hip (Z = −0.595) and both knees (left, Z = −0.628; right,
Z = −1.126) and ankles (left, Z = −1.534; right, Z = −1.142) after six weeks of training
camp, p > .05.

Discussion and implications
We aimed to identify the joint power contribution changes during a speed running bout
in American style football players before and after participating in a six-week NFL draft
preparation camp. The camp included focused drills for developing linear speed (Table 1)
as well as resistance training and position specific drills. Players were highly skilled with

35% invited to attend the prestigious combine and the remaining 65% performing for
scouts and coaches at what are called ‘pro days’. We hoped to gain insight into joint-
specific mechanistic adaptations that would provide valuable information for what
change is possible in high calibre team sport athletes attempting to enhance linear
speed. Previous studies have assessed joint power redistribution during fatiguing or
exhaustive runs (Melaro et al., 2021; Willer et al., 2021), changing stride mechanics
and/or speed (Belli et al., 2002; Dewald et al., 2023; Schache et al., 2011), between
recreational and competitive runners (Sanno et al., 2018), and in older runners (Kim &
Park, 2022). However, to our knowledge no studies have documented differences before
and after a training block in highly skilled athletes. We hypothesised that participation in
training camp would redistribute both positive and negative joint power from the ankle
towards the more proximal hip joint and knee joints even if treadmill speed were kept
uniform between testing sessions. The hypothesis was partially accepted.

477	Interestingly, while the magnitudes of positive ankle power showed virtually no change at

482	m/s (Dorn et al., 2012, Schache et al., 2001; Schache et al., 2015). The mean run test speed
483	in the current study was 6.4 m/s and was the same for both testing sessions. Muscles
484	around the hip appear to have generated greater work during the propulsion phase
485	(Figure 6) just as occurs with running at faster speeds. This may be a marker of improved
486	limb efficiency. However, the effect sizes were small (left, r = .24; right, r = .20). Further,

488	to 6.0 W/kg. A runner may become more reliant upon hip muscles if unable to generate
489	power through the calf muscles (van Oeveren et al., 2024). This has been shown to occur

546	Greater muscle damage occurs with cumulative negative work, or eccentric loads
547	(Hashizume et al., 2019). Thus, this finding was seen as not only potentially enhancing
548	for performance but also increasing injury protection. Further, ground contact times
549	have been found to be relatively consistent up to 20 km/hr and then may vary with lesser
550	skilled runners demonstrating an inability to generate high braking and propulsive forces
551	in a short time by the muscles. Participants increased hip and knee negative power during
552	braking period and increased hip positive power during propulsion. Enhancements in
553	swing leg mechanics, specifically ‘leg retraction’ may have influenced the findings for
554	negative joint power. Leg retraction is the rearward leg rotation before initial ground
555	contact and is controlled primarily by hip rotation (Orendurff et al., 2018) with the
556	extensors as prime forward movers of the body (Belli et al., 2002). Leg retraction
557	enhances running mechanics by reducing horizontal velocity difference of the foot
558	relative to the surface (Blazevich, 2017; Blum et al., 2010). This reduces impact impulse,
559	prevents slipping (Karssen et al., 2015), improves stability (Blum et al., 2010; Karssen et
560	al., 2011), and possibly decreases total limb negative power, specifically at the ankle.
561	Decreases in negative power have been shown to result from improved muscle-tendon
562	elasticity and stiffness (Hirayama et al., 2017; Kubo et al., 2010, 2012), stride mechanics
563	(Swinnen et al., 2021), and neuromuscular control (Akbar et al., 2022). Thus, this change
564	may be a training adaptation reflective of enhanced linear speed mechanics. However, all
565	players did not exhibit this shift. Seventeen (~33%) participants had 0.5 to 9 W/kg
566	increases in negative hip joint power and five (~10%) had ≥ 9 W/kg increases in negative
567	ankle joint power. Intervention programs of ≥12 weeks have been shown to be most
568	beneficial to muscle-tendon adaptation (Bohm et al., 2015; Hirayama et al., 2017) while
569	stride mechanics and neuromuscular control programs may induce beneficial changes in
570	performance in 2–8 weeks (Akbar et al., 2022; Barber-Westin et al., 2015; Maćkała &
571	Fostiak, 2015). Thus, it is plausible that the sprint technique drills, and the other related
572	camp exercises may have reduced the need of the ankle joint’s muscle-tendon complex
573	for energy absorption for most of the participants. To illustrate, the first five linear speed
574	drills in Table 1 focus on rapid ankle dorsiflexion at foot-off and piston-like motion at the
575	hips and knees. Improvements in force application mechanics may have aided in redis­

577	as offensive and defensive linemen. However, position differences were not evaluated in
578	the current study. This group began training camp with most participants just finishing
579	their competitive playing season where mechanics of game specific demands such as
580	changes of direction and large decelerations were predominant for most player positions.
581	The goal of training camp was to prepare participants for their professional try-out in
582	which they showcase linear speed in the 36.6 m run.

587	training camp protocol. Footwear differences between testing sessions, muscle
588	soreness, fatigue, energy intake, limb dominance, or previous injury may have

603	Conclusion
604	This study is the first to longitudinally examine changes in joint-level power
605	magnitude and contribution during speed running before and after a training
606	block in a group of highly skilled athletes. The goal was to gain insight into joint-
607	specific mechanistic adaptations that would provide valuable information for what
608	is possible in high calibre team sport athletes attempting to enhance linear speed.
609	The primary generator of both positive and negative joint power was the ankle,
610	and this was consistent with previous findings (Swinnen et al., 2021). Positive
611	power contribution at the ankle decreased by ~ 0.5% and increased at the hip by ~
612	1.0%, but these were not significant. The interesting change was that of decreased
613	negative ankle power bilaterally indicating less reliance on the ankle’s muscle-
614	tendon complex for energy absorption during the first portion of the stance phase.
615	This change occurred despite running at the same speed (mean 6.4 m/s) before
616	and after training camp. The distal-to-proximal shift in negative joint power as a
617	by-product of training requires further investigation. Given that the high skill of
618	the participants may affect the sensitivity of change of the variables in this study,
619	the moderate and low effect sizes produced may still warrant attention. We also
620	observed individual differences in the training response that might have affected
621	the results. Further, future researchers may consider examining adaptations
622	between player position groups. We suggest that the American style football
623	players in the current study may have adopted the joint power mechanics of
624	those exhibited when running at faster speeds and this could be considered a
625	training attribute.

Since faster running speeds have been shown to change joint power contribution (Jin
& Hahn, 2018, Schache et al., 2001; Schache et al., 2015), treadmill speed was controlled
between testing sessions to aid in distinguishing camp participation effects on the
dependent variables. The joint power magnitudes in the current study are comparable
to those from similar speed runs in previous studies (Belli et al., 2002; Kariyama & Zushi,
2016) and show the ankle to be the dominant power producer bilaterally for both
absorption (~50%) and release (~65%) (Belli et al., 2002; Schache et al., 2015; Stearne
et al., 2014). Total positive power did not change for both limbs after training camp.

Interestingly, while the magnitudes of positive ankle power showed virtually no change at
the post-run, there was a minor reduction (~0.5 %) in positive ankle contribution to total
limb power that appears to be the result of small mean increases in positive hip power
magnitude (0.55–0.75 W/kg) that shifted the contribution. This is an intriguing finding
since hip power has been shown to increase with cumulative running speeds above ~7.0
m/s (Dorn et al., 2012, Schache et al., 2001; Schache et al., 2015). The mean run test speed
in the current study was 6.4 m/s and was the same for both testing sessions. Muscles
around the hip appear to have generated greater work during the propulsion phase
(Figure 6) just as occurs with running at faster speeds. This may be a marker of improved
limb efficiency. However, the effect sizes were small (left, r = .24; right, r = .20). Further,
not all participants increased positive hip joint power. Ten players (19%) decreased by 0.5
to 6.0 W/kg. A runner may become more reliant upon hip muscles if unable to generate
power through the calf muscles (van Oeveren et al., 2024). This has been shown to occur
when runners shift to a higher step frequency at a lower speed (van Oeveren et al., 2024)
which also lowers ground contact time. Subjects in the current study decreased their
ground contact times on the left side from 160 ms to 158 ms and maintained 158 ms on
the right side at both testing runs leading to symmetrical ground contact times. Limb
symmetry has been the subject of biomechanical analyses of sprint (Exell et al., 2017;
Exell et al., 2012; Kaçoğlu, 2019) and distance (Gao et al., 2020, Hashizume et al., 2019;
Vial et al., 2023) runners. Exell et al. (2017) examined relationships between various

kinetic, kinematic, strength (squat jump GRFs), and performance asymmetries in eight
male competitive sprinters. Results showed the asymmetries were highly individual and
there were no significant relationships except for ankle work during sprint running and
peak vertical force (r = .895) and power (r = .761) during the squat jumps. The research­
ers suggested that the ankle joint may be vital in regulating asymmetry in sprinting.
Symmetry in joint power contributions were not examined in the current study.
However, Table 3 shows minimal differences (~1–1.5%) in mean joint contribution
values show between the right and left ankles. During sprinting, the ankle joint plays
an important role in producing the necessary large vertical ground reaction force (vGRF)
(Dorn et al., 2012; Schache et al., 2014; Stefanyshyn & Nigg, 1998), reducing ground
contact time (Charalambous et al., 2002), and enhancing mechanical efficiency
(Kuitunen et al., 2002). Specifically, the ankle plantar flexor muscles (gastrocnemius
and soleus) have a dominant role in those tasks and rely greatly on the utilisation of
tendon elastic strain energy for generating power during the stance phase. In the current
study, mean stance-averaged vGRFs were unchanged for the left (pre, 18.39 ± 1.38 vs.
post, 18.47 ± 1.33 N/kg) and right (pre, 18.37 ± 1.78 vs. 18.28 ± 1.61 N/kg) limbs which
seems congruent with the stability of the magnitudes of positive total limb power.
   Total limb negative power decreased after training and was statistically significant for
the left limb with a medium effect size (r = .30). The reduction may indicate an improved
ability to absorb energy in the initial part of stance. Significant decreases in negative ankle
power magnitude influenced this finding. Most of the power absorbed relative to the total

limb power (~47–51%) at both testing sessions was performed around the ankle joint.
Greater muscle damage occurs with cumulative negative work, or eccentric loads
(Hashizume et al., 2019). Thus, this finding was seen as not only potentially enhancing
for performance but also increasing injury protection. Further, ground contact times
have been found to be relatively consistent up to 20 km/hr and then may vary with lesser
skilled runners demonstrating an inability to generate high braking and propulsive forces
in a short time by the muscles. Participants increased hip and knee negative power during
braking period and increased hip positive power during propulsion. Enhancements in
swing leg mechanics, specifically ‘leg retraction’ may have influenced the findings for
negative joint power. Leg retraction is the rearward leg rotation before initial ground
contact and is controlled primarily by hip rotation (Orendurff et al., 2018) with the
extensors as prime forward movers of the body (Belli et al., 2002). Leg retraction
enhances running mechanics by reducing horizontal velocity difference of the foot
relative to the surface (Blazevich, 2017; Blum et al., 2010). This reduces impact impulse,
prevents slipping (Karssen et al., 2015), improves stability (Blum et al., 2010; Karssen et
al., 2011), and possibly decreases total limb negative power, specifically at the ankle.
Decreases in negative power have been shown to result from improved muscle-tendon
elasticity and stiffness (Hirayama et al., 2017; Kubo et al., 2010, 2012), stride mechanics
(Swinnen et al., 2021), and neuromuscular control (Akbar et al., 2022). Thus, this change
may be a training adaptation reflective of enhanced linear speed mechanics. However, all
players did not exhibit this shift. Seventeen (~33%) participants had 0.5 to 9 W/kg
increases in negative hip joint power and five (~10%) had ≥ 9 W/kg increases in negative
ankle joint power. Intervention programs of ≥12 weeks have been shown to be most
beneficial to muscle-tendon adaptation (Bohm et al., 2015; Hirayama et al., 2017) while
stride mechanics and neuromuscular control programs may induce beneficial changes in
performance in 2–8 weeks (Akbar et al., 2022; Barber-Westin et al., 2015; Maćkała &
Fostiak, 2015). Thus, it is plausible that the sprint technique drills, and the other related
camp exercises may have reduced the need of the ankle joint’s muscle-tendon complex
for energy absorption for most of the participants. To illustrate, the first five linear speed
drills in Table 1 focus on rapid ankle dorsiflexion at foot-off and piston-like motion at the
hips and knees. Improvements in force application mechanics may have aided in redis­
tributing joint power especially for players of positions where sprinting is required such
as offensive and defensive linemen. However, position differences were not evaluated in
the current study. This group began training camp with most participants just finishing
their competitive playing season where mechanics of game specific demands such as
changes of direction and large decelerations were predominant for most player positions.
The goal of training camp was to prepare participants for their professional try-out in
which they showcase linear speed in the 36.6 m run.
    The unique participant pool, elite-level American style football players training
for the NFL draft at a single facility presented an opportunity to monitor a highly
specialised sample but also made it difficult to utilise a control group. Without a
control group, we cannot be confident that the observations were solely from the
training camp protocol. Footwear differences between testing sessions, muscle
soreness, fatigue, energy intake, limb dominance, or previous injury may have
influenced the findings. However, it should be noted that training camp protocols
for resistance training, field-drills, sleep, nutritional supplements, recovery
 14      G. M. MOKHA ET AL.


treatment, corrective exercises, and injury management are strict and consistent
strengthening findings within pre-post test limitations. Furthermore, 43/52 (83%)
of the participants were categorised as Skill (e.g., wide receivers, defensive backs)
or Big-skill (e.g., tight ends, linebackers) who run the ball more in American style
football. The remaining were Big players (linemen) who primarily block and
tackle. Thus, the small to moderate r effect sizes observed may have been
influenced by player position.


Conclusion
This study is the first to longitudinally examine changes in joint-level power
magnitude and contribution during speed running before and after a training
block in a group of highly skilled athletes. The goal was to gain insight into joint-
specific mechanistic adaptations that would provide valuable information for what
is possible in high calibre team sport athletes attempting to enhance linear speed.
The primary generator of both positive and negative joint power was the ankle,
and this was consistent with previous findings (Swinnen et al., 2021). Positive
power contribution at the ankle decreased by ~ 0.5% and increased at the hip by ~
1.0%, but these were not significant. The interesting change was that of decreased
negative ankle power bilaterally indicating less reliance on the ankle’s muscle-
tendon complex for energy absorption during the first portion of the stance phase.
This change occurred despite running at the same speed (mean 6.4 m/s) before
and after training camp. The distal-to-proximal shift in negative joint power as a
by-product of training requires further investigation. Given that the high skill of
the participants may affect the sensitivity of change of the variables in this study,
the moderate and low effect sizes produced may still warrant attention. We also
observed individual differences in the training response that might have affected
the results. Further, future researchers may consider examining adaptations
between player position groups. We suggest that the American style football
players in the current study may have adopted the joint power mechanics of
those exhibited when running at faster speeds and this could be considered a
training attribute.

    REVIEW ARTICLE



Training for Muscular Strength: Methods for Monitoring and Adjusting
Training Intensity
Timothy J. Suchomel1           · Sophia Nimphius2 · Christopher R. Bellon3 · W. Guy Hornsby4 · Michael H. Stone5

Accepted: 17 May 2021
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2021


Abstract
Linear loading, the two-for-two rule, percent of one repetition maximum (1RM), RM zones, rate of perceived exertion
(RPE), repetitions in reserve, set-repetition best, autoregulatory progressive resistance exercise (APRE), and velocity-based
training (VBT) are all methods of adjusting resistance training intensity. Each method has advantages and disadvantages
that strength and conditioning practitioners should be aware of when measuring and monitoring strength characteristics.
The linear loading and 2-for-2 methods may be beneficial for novice athletes; however, they may be limited in their capac-
ity to provide athletes with variation and detrimental if used exclusively for long periods of time. The percent of 1RM and
RM zone methods may provide athletes with more variation and greater potential for strength–power adaptations; however,
they fail to account for daily changes in athlete’s performance capabilities. An athlete’s daily readiness can be addressed
to various extents by both subjective (e.g., RPE, repetitions in reserve, set-repetition best, and APRE) and objective (e.g.,
VBT) load adjustment methods. Future resistance training monitoring may aim to include a combination of measures that
quantify outcome (e.g., velocity, load, time, etc.) with process (e.g., variability, coordination, efficiency, etc.) relevant to
the stage of learning or the task being performed. Load adjustment and monitoring methods should be used to supplement
and guide the practitioner, quantify what the practitioner ‘sees’, and provide longitudinal data to assist in reviewing athlete
development and providing baselines for the rate of expected development in resistance training when an athlete returns to
sport from injury or large training load reductions.



                                                                                  Key Points

                                                                                  Linear loading, the 2-for-2 method, percentage of one
                                                                                  repetition maximum, and repetition maximum zone
                                                                                  training may not serve as effective methods for monitor-
                                                                                  ing resistance training intensity as they fail to account for
                                                                                  daily changes in an athlete’s performance capabilities.

 "sourceFile":"Training for muscular strength - Methods for monitoring and adjusting training intensity.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'Training for Muscular Strength: Methods for Monitoring and Adjusting Training Intensity' matches the filename title.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain":"Training & Performance",
 "domains":["Training & Performance","Monitoring & Technology"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Coaching","Rehabilitation"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Narrative review of methods for adjusting resistance training intensity: linear loading, the two-for-two rule, percent of 1RM, repetition maximum zones, RPE and repetitions in reserve, set-repetition best, autoregulatory progressive resistance exercise (APRE), and velocity-based training (VBT). The authors weigh each method's advantages and limits and propose combining outcome measures (such as velocity) with process measures of motor learning. No sample or pooled effect is reported, and the cited comparison studies are described only in summary.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The review does not describe a literature search or selection process, so the evidence base and the authors' method preferences cannot be checked. Several cited comparisons are small, use student or thesis samples, or compare methods mainly against linear loading, which limits how far the ranking of methods can be relied on.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat the review's preferred methods, such as APRE, set-repetition best and VBT, as proven superior to other loading methods, when the cited comparisons are few, often small, and mostly against linear loading.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2021,
   "citation":"Suchomel TJ, Nimphius S, Bellon CR, Hornsby WG, Stone MH. Training for Muscular Strength: Methods for Monitoring and Adjusting Training Intensity. Sports Med. 2021.",
   "doi":"10.1007/s40279-021-01488-9",
   "abstract":"This review compares methods for adjusting resistance training intensity, including linear loading, the two-for-two rule, percent of one repetition maximum, repetition maximum zones, rating of perceived exertion and repetitions in reserve, set-repetition best, autoregulatory progressive resistance exercise and velocity-based training. The authors conclude that methods which account for daily readiness, such as RPE, repetitions in reserve, set-repetition best, APRE and velocity-based training, can be combined with outcome and process measures to guide practitioners.",
   "tldr":"No single intensity method suits every athlete. Linear loading and fixed percentages of 1RM miss daily readiness, while RPE, set-repetition best, APRE and velocity-based training adjust to it. Combining these with longer-term monitoring is the authors' recommendation.",
   "methods":"Narrative review of resistance training intensity methods, covering the advantages, limitations and practical use of each method. The review also discusses how motor learning and process measures could be added to outcome-based monitoring. No search strategy is described.",
   "findings":"The authors report that linear loading can produce a plateau or overreaching if used for long periods, and that %1RM and RM zones fail to account for daily fluctuations in performance. They describe RPE, repetitions in reserve, set-repetition best, APRE and velocity-based training as more responsive to daily readiness, and cite comparison studies in which APRE and set-repetition best produced strength gains similar to or greater than linear loading or RM zones in some trials.",
   "limitations":"No systematic search or quality appraisal is described, so the selection of studies is not transparent. The cited comparisons vary in design, sample and method of RPE or velocity measurement, and the authors note that RPE and repetitions in reserve accuracy and velocity-based 1RM prediction are not yet established across populations.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use outcome measures (such as load and velocity) alongside subjective readiness measures, rather than a single fixed-percentage prescription, and be cautious with novices, since RPE accuracy depends on experience. Keep track of longer-term training volume and intensity so that stagnation or overreaching can be spotted.",
   "athleteDev":"Strength coaches can combine RPE or repetitions in reserve with velocity-based or set-repetition best methods to adjust loads from day to day, while watching for technique loss near failure. The review gives a framework for choosing methods, not a tested ranking of their effects on strength.",
   "rtp":"The review mentions rehabilitation and return from injury only in passing, and it does not evaluate return-to-sport decisions. It cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria or to judge when an athlete's strength is ready for sport."
 }
}

   "citation":"Marvin LA, Read P, McLean B, Palmer S, Fransen J. Training Interventions for Improved Deceleration Ability in Adult Team-Based Field Sports Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Literature. Int J Strength Cond. 2024.",
   "doi":"10.47206/ijsc.v4i1.313",
   "abstract":"Twelve randomised controlled trials in adult team field and court athletes were reviewed, and nine were pooled across 29 deceleration-specific outcomes. Training interventions did not improve deceleration performance compared with control groups (SMD -0.04, 95% CI -0.50 to 0.42), and the risk of bias was high in all studies.",
   "tldr":"Current randomised trials do not show that general training improves deceleration performance in team athletes more than usual training does. Because these trials used mostly non-specific interventions and had high risk of bias, the result is inconclusive rather than a verdict against deceleration training.",
   "methods":"Systematic search of SPORTDiscus, PubMed and Web of Science, followed by PRISMA-guided screening (registered on OSF) for randomised controlled trials with a control group and pre-post deceleration outcomes in adult team-field and court athletes. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2, and post-intervention Hedges g values were pooled using a multilevel random-effects model with Knapp-Hartung confidence intervals.",
   "findings":"Across all deceleration performance outcomes, the pooled SMD was -0.04 (95% CI -0.50 to 0.42), with negative values favouring control groups and I2 = 0%. Secondary kinetic outcomes favoured control groups (SMD -0.29, 95% CI -0.83 to 0.25; joint kinetics -0.20), joint kinematics slightly favoured interventions (SMD 0.07, 95% CI -0.11 to 0.24), and muscle activation favoured control groups (SMD -0.10, 95% CI -0.44 to 0.24). None of these pooled secondary effects was statistically significant.",
   "limitations":"Only 12 small RCTs were found, nine were pooled, and most outcomes were measured in one or two studies. All studies had high overall risk of bias, and the pooled outcomes came from different protocols and definitions. The text reports 380 participants, while the abstract reports 381.",
   "practicalImplications":"The evidence does not yet show that general strength, plyometric or agility work improves deceleration more than usual training. Practitioners who want better deceleration should target it directly, with braking-specific or sport-representative drills, and measure it with consistent outcomes.",
   "athleteDev":"Do not assume that adding general strength, plyometric or agility blocks will improve how athletes decelerate. If deceleration is a priority, plan deceleration-specific work and track it with the same test each time, since current trials do not identify a reliable method.",
   "rtp":"This review does not inform return to sport. It included healthy trained athletes in intervention trials and did not study injured players or return-to-play criteria."
 }
}

                    Training Load and Acute Performance Decrements
                           Following Different Training Sessions
                          Kobe M. Vermeire,1 Kevin Caen,1,2 Jan G. Bourgois,1,2 and Jan Boone1,2
   1
    Department of Movement and Sports Sciences, Ghent University, Ghent, Belgium; 2Center of Sports Medicine, Ghent University Hospital, Ghent, Belgium

       Purpose: To examine the differences in training load (TL) metrics when quantifying training sessions differing in intensity and
       duration. The relationship between the TL metrics and the acute performance decrement measured immediately after the sessions
       was also assessed. Methods: Eleven male recreational cyclists performed 4 training sessions in a random order, immediately
       followed by a 3-km time trial (TT). Before this period, participants performed the time TT in order to obtain a baseline
       performance. The difference in the average power output for the TTs following the training sessions was then expressed relative
       to the best baseline performance. The training sessions were quantiﬁed using 7 different TL metrics, 4 using heart rate as input, 2
       using power output, and 1 using the rating of perceived exertion. Results: The load of the sessions was estimated differently
       depending on the TL metrics used. Also, within the metrics using the same input (heart rate and power), differences were found.
       TL using the rating of perceived exertion was the only metric showing a response that was consistent with the acute performance
       decrements found for the different training sessions. The Training Stress Score and the individualized training impulse
       demonstrated similar patterns but overexpressed the intensity of the training sessions. The total work done resulted in an
       overrepresentation of the duration of training. Conclusion: TL metrics provide dissimilar results as to which training sessions
       have higher loads. The load based on TL using the rating of perceived exertion was the only one in line with the acute
       performance decrements found in this study.

       Keywords: cycling, quantiﬁcation, interval, training stress, training impulse

      The authors aimed to quantify (a) the periodization of physical loading and daily carbohydrate (CHO) intake across an in-season
      weekly microcycle of Australian Football and (b) the quantity and source of CHO consumed during game play and training.
      Physical loading (via global positioning system technology) and daily CHO intake (via a combination of 24-hr recall, food
      diaries, and remote food photographic method) were assessed in 42 professional male players during two weekly microcycles
      comprising a home and away ﬁxture. The players also reported the source and quantity of CHO consumed during all games
      (n = 22 games) and on the training session completed 4 days before each game (n = 22 sessions). The total distance was greater
      (p < .05) on game day (GD; 13 km) versus all training days. The total distance differed between training days, where GD-2 (8 km)
      was higher than GD-1, GD-3, and GD-4 (3.5, 0, and 7 km, respectively). The daily CHO intake was also different between
      training days, with reported intakes of 1.8, 1.4, 2.5, and 4.5 g/kg body mass on GD-4, GD-3, GD-2, and GD-1, respectively. The
      CHO intake was greater (p < .05) during games (59 ± 19 g) compared with training (1 ± 1 g), where in the former, 75% of the
      CHO consumed was from ﬂuids as opposed to gels. Although the data suggest that Australian Football players practice elements
      of CHO periodization, the low absolute CHO intakes likely represent considerable underreporting in this population. Even when
      accounting for potential underreporting, the data also suggest Australian Football players underconsume CHO in relation to the
      physical demands of training and competition.

      Keywords: GPS, sports drinks, sports gels

GPS load was recorded, and carbohydrate intake was self-reported through 24-hour recall, food diaries and remote food photography. Total distance was highest on game day, and self-reported carbohydrate intake was highest on the day before a game (4.3 g/kg home, 4.8 g/kg away) and lowest on the day with no training (1.5 g/kg home, 1.4 g/kg away).  "screeningLimitations":"Carbohydrate intake was self-reported, and the authors state that the values probably underestimate true intake. The data cover two microcycles at one club, and game-day carbohydrate data came from 22 games and 22 selected players, so the findings describe one squad over a short period.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could take the self-reported carbohydrate figures as the squad's actual intake and conclude that players underfuel by a fixed amount, when the authors state that the recalls are likely underreported and were not checked against measured intake.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2020,
   "citation":"Routledge HE, Graham S, Di Michele R, Burgess D, Erskine RM, Close GL, Morton JP. Training Load and Carbohydrate Periodization Practices of Elite Male Australian Football Players: Evidence of Fueling for the Work Required. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2020;30(4):280-286.",
   "doi":"10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0311",
   "abstract":"In 42 professional Australian football players over two in-season microcycles, GPS load was highest on game day and self-reported carbohydrate intake varied across the week, peaking the day before games. Carbohydrate intake during games was much higher than during training, mostly from fluids, but the authors conclude that the reported intakes are low and probably underreported.",
   "tldr":"Australian football players appear to vary carbohydrate intake with the weekly training load, eating most the day before a game. Their reported intakes are still low for the workload, and the carbohydrate recalls are probably underestimates.",
   "methods":"Forty-two players were studied across a home and an away microcycle in the 2017 season. GPS (Optimeye S5, 10 Hz) recorded total distance, running, high-speed running and sprinting. Daily carbohydrate intake was estimated from 4-day food diaries, 24-hour recall and remote food photography, with in-game and in-training intake recalled within 30 minutes. Repeated-measures general linear models were used for day and fixture week.",
   "findings":"Total distance was greater on game day (13 km) than on all training days. Self-reported daily carbohydrate was lowest on GD-3 (1.5 g/kg home, 1.4 g/kg away) and highest on GD-1 (4.3 g/kg home, 4.8 g/kg away). During games, players consumed 59 ± 19 g of carbohydrate (34 ± 11 g/h, 75% from fluids), while training intake was 1 ± 1 g. Fifty-three percent of players reached the 30 to 60 g/h range during games.",
   "limitations":"Intake was self-reported and probably underestimated, and the authors could not separate deliberate from habitual choices. The sample is one club over two microcycles, and game-day carbohydrate data came from 22 games. The abstract gives daily intakes of 1.8, 1.4, 2.5 and 4.5 g/kg, which do not match Table 2 (for example 2.1 and 1.8 g/kg on GD-4), and the discussion gives 5 g/kg on GD-1 rather than the table values.",
   "practicalImplications":"Players may need education on carbohydrate needs on training days and on high-load days before games, not only on the day before a match. Match intake of 30 to 60 g/h is achievable with fluids and gels, and the authors suggest that intake should be checked with methods more accurate than recall.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: Plan carbohydrate intake around the weekly load, so that high-load training days get more fuel than the current pattern suggests, and build match-day intake toward 30 to 60 g/h with fluids or gels. Use a more objective method than recall when monitoring intake, since self-report probably understates it.",
